items.title: Machine Learning-Augmented Precision Dosing: Integrating Pharmacokinetic Modeling With Clinical Decision Support.
items.abstract_or_text: Inter-individual variability in drug exposure can lead to ineffective therapy or toxicity, particularly in vulnerable patients. Routine model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) relies mainly on population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models, Bayesian forecasting, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM). Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling has a complementary role in extrapolation to special populations, evaluation of drug-drug interactions, and simulation of unobserved scenarios, but it remains uncommon for bedside dose adjustment. Machine learning (ML) may provide additional support when critical illness, organ dysfunction, or polypharmacy creates complex nonlinear relationships. The increasing availability of electronic health records, real-world data, and high-dimensional biomedical datasets has accelerated interest in ML for precision dosing. ML can support exposure prediction, limited-sampling AUC estimation, outcome-risk stratification, and monitoring prioritization. Its clinical role depends on the decision target, the availability of concentration data, and whether pharmacological constraints are retained within the modeling architecture. This review covers direct prediction models, limited-sampling AUC estimators, hybrid pharmacometric-ML models, neural ordinary differential equation approaches, and reinforcement learning for sequential dose decisions. We examine data sources, feature engineering, validation, reporting, and governance across glycopeptides, beta-lactams, polymyxins, triazole antifungals, and immunosuppressants. We also describe a staged clinical workflow in which concentration measurements and mechanistic models are used to calibrate data-driven predictions, and we identify the evidence needed for clinical implementation.

items.title: Atherosclerosis and Diabetic Foot Share a Common Molecular Signature of Cellular Senescence: A Multi-Omics and Machine Learning Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Atherosclerosis (AS) and diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) are two major vascular complications of diabetes that frequently co-exist, yet whether they share a common molecular basis remains unclear. Here, we tested the hypothesis that AS and DFU share a common senescence-related molecular signature. We integrated transcriptomic datasets GSE134431 (DFU) and GSE163154 (AS), identified differentially expressed genes common to both diseases, and intersected them with the CellAge senescence-associated gene set to obtain senescence-related DEGs (SR-DEGs). Three machine learning algorithms—LASSO, random forest, and SVM-RFE—were applied to prioritize core feature genes, which were subsequently validated at the single-cell (GSE245703), tissue, and in vitro levels. We identified 72 SR-DEGs shared by AS and DFU, from which three core feature genes—CALCOCO1, CCND2, and FUCA1—were selected by cross-algorithm consensus. A multi-gene nomogram incorporating these genes achieved excellent discriminative performance in both diseases (AUC: 0.96 for DFU, 0.90 for AS). Single-cell analysis revealed cell type–restricted expression patterns of these genes, with fibroblasts emerging as a key senescent cell type in the DFU microenvironment. Clinical validation in an independent cohort of 22 patients (11 DFU vs. 11 non-diabetic foot ulcer) confirmed significant accumulation of senescent cells and dysregulated feature gene expression in DFU tissues. Moreover, metformin treatment effectively attenuated hydrogen peroxide- and high-glucose/high-lipid-induced fibroblast senescence in vitro, partially reversing the expression changes of the three feature genes. These findings demonstrate that AS and DFU share a common senescence-associated molecular signature, identify CALCOCO1, CCND2, and FUCA1 as potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets, and suggest that metformin may exert protective effects through modulation of this senescence-related gene network.

items.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
items.abstract_or_text: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

items.title: FateDriver: Weakly supervised dual-view graph learning for transition-specific prioritization of candidate regulators in cellular reprogramming
items.abstract_or_text: Cellular reprogramming supports regenerative medicine, yet the endogenous regulators of a specified source-to-target transition remain incompletely defined. Existing computational methods rank candidate regulators from network topology, trajectory dynamics, or cell-state labels, leaving unused the factors experimentally delivered to induce the transition. We present FateDriver, a weakly supervised dual-view graph neural network that jointly represents cells and genes from single-cell transcriptomes, treats the delivered factors as sparse gene-level labels, and ranks the remaining genes for a specified transition under a positive--unlabeled formulation. Across two OSKM datasets and one GMT dataset, FateDriver ranked first or second among six methods in recovering externally curated reference genes, exceeded a supervision-matched non-graph model despite weaker co-expression with the delivered factors, and achieved the highest recovery of protein targets of pluripotency-inducing chemical cocktails in both OSKM datasets. Holding either the source or the endpoint fixed yielded distinct candidate programs, including a DDX58 --interferon axis associated with cells lacking endogenous pluripotency markers. Applying the same framework to candidate source--target pairs prioritized distinct candidate origins for two in vivo partially reprogrammed intestinal populations. FateDriver converts sparse experimental knowledge into transition-specific hypotheses for regulator prioritization from single-cell trajectories.

items.title: Development of a Deep Learning Model Integrating Computed Tomography Images and Blood Data for the Diagnosis of Acute Cholecystitis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence-based diagnostic model for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis (AC) using non-contrast CT images and clinical data. Methods This retrospective study included 197 patients (100 AC, 97 non-AC) treated between January 2016 and December 2025 at a single center. Patients were randomly divided into training (n = 139) and test (n = 58) datasets. Three models were constructed: an imaging-based deep learning model, a clinical data-based machine learning model, and a hybrid machine learning model integrating deep learning-derived imaging features with clinical data. CT images were preprocessed, and gallbladder regions were segmented. Clinical variables included white blood cell counts and levels of C-reactive protein and liver function markers. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Statistical comparisons were performed using Welch's t-test and Chi-square test. Results The imaging-based model achieved accuracy 0.741, precision 0.703, recall 0.867, specificity 0.607, F1 score 0.776, and AUC 0.863. The blood-based model achieved accuracy 0.914, precision 0.931, recall 0.900, specificity 0.929, F1 score 0.915, and AUC 0.946. The hybrid model showed the highest performance, with accuracy 0.931, precision 0.882, recall 1.000, specificity 0.857, F1 score 0.938, and AUC 0.996. Conclusions A hybrid model integrating CT imaging and clinical data improved diagnostic performance for AC compared with single-modality models.

items.title: Identification of Non-Invasive Tumor-specific Biomarkers for Hepatocellular Carcinoma through Multi-transcriptomics Data Integration
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most prevalent primary liver cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Early detection is critical for improving patient outcomes; however, current surveillance modalities exhibit insufficient sensitivity for early-stage disease. While tissue biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard, its invasive nature limits its routine application. This study seeks to identify non-invasive blood-based biomarkers for HCC through transcriptomic analysis. Methods We analyzed transcriptomic datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), focusing on HCC tissues, plasma, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) and differential expression profiling were employed to identify candidate biomarkers, with key genes prioritized using STRING network analysis. Additionally, exosomal miRNA profiles were integrated to capture systemic regulatory signatures. Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted via Reactome 2024 to identify consistently dysregulated "tissue fundamental pathways" across liver datasets, which were then compared with blood-derived pathways. Candidate genes within these pathways were analyzed to define potential blood-based biomarker panels. Results We identified 11 plasma-derived genes (e.g., RPS27A, CCND1, HSP90AB1, POLR2F, H2BC13, H2BC14, POLR2C, POLR2L, NPM1, FEN1, XRCC6), 6 PBMC-derived genes (e.g., JUN, POLR2H, CUL1, DICER1, AURKA, CCNA1), and 9 exosomal miRNAs (e.g., hsa-miR-671-5p, hsa-miR-184, hsa-miR-425-5p, hsa-miR-193a-5p, hsa-miR-103a-3p, hsa-miR-371a-5p, hsa-miR-874-3p, hsa-miR-663a, hsa-miR-18a-5p) significantly correlated with HCC. Many identified biomarkers align with established cancer hallmark pathways, underscoring their mechanistic relevance. Notably, several of these genes (e.g., JUN, POLR2C) and miRNAs (e.g., miR-874-3p) have not been previously reported in association with HCC, highlighting their potential as novel biomarker candidates. Conclusion This integrative multi-transcriptomic analysis has unveiled novel, clinically relevant blood-based biomarkers for HCC, providing a promising foundation for sensitive, non-invasive detection strategies. Prospective validation in clinical cohorts is crucial for advancing the translation of these findings into early diagnostic protocols.

items.title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design: Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects: 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior- and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods: Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures: Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results: For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions: Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

items.title: An agent-built, verified atlas of public spatial transcriptomics shows that breadth across studies drives transfer and reproducibility
items.abstract_or_text: Public spatial transcriptomics data are deposited study by study, in formats that differ from one laboratory to the next, and no resource has yet indexed or verified them as a whole. Here we present SpatialDataAgent-DB, an atlas built from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) by SpatialDataAgent, a workflow in which language-model agents do the work and every output is checked rather than trusted. An assay index covering all 298,179 GEO series identifies 2,411 spatial series, which gives public spatial data an explicit denominator. For each series, an agent writes conversion code instead of editing the data directly, and a frozen, rule-based scorer recomputes every released value from the source files. In a held-out test, the scorer rejected all 1,231 corrupted copies. We also visually reviewed every released sample, including the 4,386 H&E-registered Visium samples of our earlier HESRT release. SpatialDataAgent-DB contains 12,163 samples from 12 platforms and 42 species in a single format, each with its provenance and defect flags. Its 8,211 image-paired samples are 5.9 times as many as in the next image-paired resource, and at least 71% of all samples are absent from five existing catalogues. Without batch correction, sequencing-based samples group by organ more than by platform: with platforms balanced, organ explains 32% of the variance of human pseudobulk profiles and platform 13% (mouse, 47% and 18%). We then used the atlas in two applications. Image-to-expression models trained on it transfer to unseen studies, and their accuracy rises steadily with training data and, at a fixed number of patches, with the number of training studies over the range tested (for H&E, Pearson r gains 0.0056 per doubling of training patches up to 524,288); 11 of 13 forecasts locked in advance were confirmed. Adding studies helps more than adding patches from the same studies, because each study leaves a fingerprint in its images. Intent-based search over the same index assembled 70 single-cell dementia studies, and the replication of disease signatures in held-out studies rose steadily with the number of studies (direction agreement averaged over 28 held-out studies, 63% with one study and 77% with 16). In both applications, performance kept rising with the number of independent studies, which a complete and verified atlas is built to provide.

items.title: Metabolic Screening and In Silico Investigation of Eucalyptus globulus Essential Oil Bioactives Against DENV-2 Envelope Protein.
items.abstract_or_text: The escalating prevalence of viral infectious diseases poses a significant threat to global public health. Among these, dengue virus (DENV) represents one of the most widespread arboviral infections, impacting nearly 400 million individuals annually, with severe clinical manifestations occurring in approximately 1% of cases, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO). Extensive research across both academic and industrial sectors has focused on various aspects of DENV, including its molecular virology, epidemiological patterns, transmission pathways, and therapeutic targets. The development of the tetravalent CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia) vaccine marked a critical advancement in dengue prevention. Nonetheless, emerging evidence has highlighted several limitations associated with current vaccination strategies, prompting a growing emphasis on the discovery and development of antiviral agents as alternative or complementary therapeutic options for effective dengue management. A total of 14 major bioactive compounds were found to be highly correlated with Dengue, yielding 70 common targets between dengue and bioactive compounds. Protein-protein interaction and network pathway analysis by KEGG and Metascape analysis show higher degree of correlation for DENV-2 targets. Molecular docking analysis shows that Globulol and Ecalyptol have higher binding affinity with two receptors, 1oke and 1tg8 f DENV-2, with binding energies of -8.3 and -7.6. Toxicity and drug-likeness analyses confirmed the safety of the metabolites for drug development. These findings suggest that Eucalyptus globulus essential oil may have potential in the treatment of dengue fever. However, further in vivo studies using animal models are required to validate its therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: Circular RNAs in Drug-Induced Cardiotoxicity: Roles, Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Potential.
items.abstract_or_text: Drug-induced cardiotoxicity (DIC) remains a major challenge in drug development and clinical practice, often resulting in treatment interruption, drug attrition, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. DIC has been associated with a wide range of therapeutic agents, including anthracyclines, HER2-targeted therapies, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and other cardiotoxic drugs. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have attracted increasing attention as stable and versatile regulatory RNAs involved in cardiovascular injury. This review summarizes the biogenesis and functional mechanisms of circRNAs, their pathological roles in DIC, biomarker potential, therapeutic implications, and translational challenges. CircRNAs regulate gene expression through diverse mechanisms, including miRNA sequestration, interactions with RNA-binding proteins, transcriptional regulation, modulation of alternative splicing, and, in some cases, peptide translation. These regulatory functions have been implicated in apoptosis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, pyroptosis, and cardiac remodeling during DIC. Emerging evidence suggests that circRNAs may serve as candidate molecular markers and potential therapeutic targets for DIC. However, the current evidence is derived predominantly from cellular and animal models, with doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity accounting for a substantial proportion of available studies. Clinical validation, particularly in well-characterized patient cohorts and across different drug classes, remains limited. Overall, further efforts are needed to establish standardized circRNA detection and quantification methods, validate their functional roles, conduct prospective clinical studies, and determine their incremental value in combination with established cardiac biomarkers before circRNA-based approaches can be translated into clinical management of DIC.

items.title: Alzheimers disease and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort.
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Young onset dementia is frequently misdiagnosed, particularly where neurodegenerative and primary psychiatric disorders (PPD) overlap. Plasma biomarkers measure current pathology, whereas polygenic risk scores (PRS) capture lifelong genetic risk. Whether PRS derived from late-onset and population samples transfer to young-onset presentations, and how they relate to plasma biomarkers, is unknown. Methods: We studied 687 participants of European ancestry from the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders (MiND) Study, a prospective young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort: 195 healthy controls (HC), 283 PPD, 55 Alzheimers disease (AD) and 154 non-AD neurodegenerative disease (oNDG). PRS for AD, a cross-disorder psychiatric factor (PSY), frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia and Parkinsons disease were computed with PRS CS, excluding the APOE locus. Plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 were available for 332 participants. Models were adjusted for age, sex and APOE e4 dose. Results: Relative to HC, the AD PRS was associated with AD (OR 1.69 per SD, 95% CI 1.17-2.45) but not PPD (0.95, 0.77-1.16). The PSY PRS showed the reciprocal pattern (PPD 1.29, 1.05-1.58; AD 1.00, 0.72-1.40). No PRS was associated with any plasma protein. In distinguishing PPD from oNDG, NfL was the strongest discriminator (OR 2.15, 1.62-2.83). The AD PRS was also associated with oNDG (1.38, 1.11-1.71), without improving discrimination (AUC 0.764 for NfL alone versus 0.773 combined). Conclusion: In young onset presentations, AD and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration. Their combined diagnostic value requires evaluation in larger, longitudinal pre-clinical cohorts.

items.title: Interpreting graph neural networks reveals microbial association patterns in inflammatory bowel diseases
items.abstract_or_text: Traditional machine learning models trained on gut microbiome abundance profiles can distinguish individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from non-IBD individuals. However, their interpretation typically considers taxa in isolation, making it difficult to understand how associations between taxa contribute to predictions. Here, we inferred individual-specific microbial association networks from longitudinal metagenomics data of 106 individuals in HMP2/iHMP and used them to train and interpret graph neural network (GNN) models, which we compared with abundance-based models such as Random Forest (RF). Although RF achieved higher predictive performance (AUPRC ~0.59 vs 0.446), interpreting the GNNs revealed that their predictions relied on a densely connected module of co-abundant Bacteroidales species. Unlike the taxa prioritized by RF, these species were not differentially abundant between conditions. In an independent cohort, this module carried most of the predictive signal, and removing its associations reduced performance to near chance. These results show that coordinated association structure, rather than abundance shifts alone, is a feature of the IBD gut microbiome, and that interpreting GNNs can uncover such patterns that complement abundance-based analyses.

items.title: Quantitative imaging of native tissue architecture combined with deep multi-omics reveals the spatial biology of kidney aging
items.abstract_or_text: Aging alters tissue architecture and metabolism in spatially heterogeneous ways, yet the connections between these measurable structural and compositional phenotypes and underlying molecular changes are largely unknown. Here, we introduce NORIGAMI (NoRI-Guided AI for Multimodal Integration), a pipeline combining Normalized Raman Imaging (NoRI), deep learning, quantitative morphology, deep proteomics, and metabolomics to investigate renal aging. Unlike conventional histology, NoRI provides label-free, scattering-corrected measurements of absolute total protein and lipid mass concentrations (mg/mL). In 32 male rats aged 9, 18, 21 and 25 months, NORIGAMI predicted the chronological age of held-out rats from NoRI images (mean absolute error 0.78 months; R^2 = 0.97), and whole-tissue images outperformed models trained on isolated tubules. Quantitative imaging identified 41 age-associated morphological and compositional features (FDR < 0.05), revealing anatomically heterogeneous and non-linear changes in lipid droplet concentration, droplet size, cytoplasmic lipid concentration and tubular architecture. Deep molecular profiling quantified 11,485 proteins and 269 metabolites, revealing coordinated declines in differentiated proximal tubule (PT) identity and oxidative metabolism, selective increases in basement-membrane collagen-IV chains, and increasing molecular heterogeneity with age. A protein clock, built mainly from extracellular-matrix and heparan-sulfate proteins, predicted age with a mean absolute error of 1.6 months. Old kidneys diverged along a dominant injury-remodeling axis, seen separately in the proteome, in kidney RNA from 54 other rats and in the metabolome, in which tubular-injury and immune proteins, including the NAD+ consuming enzyme CD38, rise as differentiated-tubule proteins and NAD+ fall. NORIGAMI subsequently linked NAD+ associated molecular changes to quantitative features of tubular geometry and protein-lipid organization, while complementary KIM-1-centered analyses identified overlapping morphological associations involving epithelial injury and lipid handling and yielded additional molecular candidates for mechanistic validation. Collectively, these findings suggest that declining tubular metabolic function, altered lipid organization and injury-associated molecular programs represent interconnected features of renal aging. NORIGAMI establishes a framework for identifying the quantitative structural manifestations of molecular aging and generating spatially informed, experimentally testable hypotheses about tissue dysfunction.

items.title: Cell-in-drop genotyping detects megabase-scale loss of heterozygosity as a quantitative marker for CRISPR-Cas9 on-target toxicity
items.abstract_or_text: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

items.title: A collaborative submission model for building high-quality data resources at scale through partnership: lessons from single-cell genomics
items.abstract_or_text: Community data resources that aggregate datasets across studies are critical infrastructure for modern biomedical research, accelerating discovery, and rapidly-advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) models place ever-greater demand on large, well-described data corpora. However, building these resources involves a fundamental tension: comprehensive metadata is imperative for reuse, yet capturing this information systematically requires substantial effort that limits growth. We detail how CZ CELLxGENE Discover has used a collaborative submission model, whereby data contributors partner with dedicated resource curators, to become a large, widely used single-cell genomics resource for diverse analytical applications including AI model development and integrative analysis. This partnership leverages contributors' intimate study knowledge and curators' focus on data reuse and expertise in standardization to improve data quality, metadata accuracy, and richness. This is achieved by motivating researcher participation through tangible benefits while minimizing submission burden. We contrast this collaborative model with contributor-driven and resource-driven approaches, highlighting tradeoffs in scalability, consistency across submissions, and quality assurance. The principles and practices we describe provide a framework for building high-quality community data resources across diverse biological data types.

items.title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Screening Framework for Efficient Eligibility Evaluation of Clinical Trial Patients
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Clinical trial patient eligibility screening is a core and labor‑intensive step in clinical research, which traditionally relies on manual review of electronic health records (EHRs) and suffers from high time costs, human errors, and inconsistent screening criteria. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), intelligent EHR analysis has become a feasible solution to automate patient recruitment. However, existing single‑LLM inference and single‑agent screening methods often fail to parse complex inclusion and exclusion rules, yielding unstable prediction and substantial false‑positive or false‑negative outputs. Methods This paper proposes a modular multi‑agent collaborative framework built upon LangGraph for clinical trial patient eligibility evaluation. The workflow is decomposed into four specialized agents. LLMs are only used for unstructured text understanding, while eligibility matching adopts deterministic rule‑driven computation to avoid LLM output randomness. Retrospective simulation experiments are conducted on an in‑house programmatically generated synthetic EHR cohort. Results Our multi‑agent framework achieves perfect accuracy, precision, recall and F1‑score on simulation cohort, outperforming the end‑to‑end single‑agent baseline. Conclusions This work provides a proof‑of‑concept intelligent automation paradigm for clinical‑trial patient screening validated on an in‑house synthetic EHR cohort; further real‑world clinical validation is required before practical clinical deployment, and the framework can be further migrated toward multicenter and cross‑border clinical trial recruitment scenarios.

items.title: Integrated single-cell transcriptomics reveal E2F1-driven multidrug resistance in medulloblastoma and identify Palbociclib as a therapeutic candidate
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Purpose Medulloblastoma (MB) is a malignant pediatric brain tumor where tumor recurrence driven by acquired multidrug resistance remains a paramount clinical challenge. Resolving the intratumoral heterogeneity underlying this resistance is urgently required to identify novel therapeutic targets. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing data and large-scale bulk transcriptomes were integrated and comprehensively analyzed. Multidrug-resistant subpopulations were identified by mapping ridge regression-based drug sensitivity predictions to single-cell profiles. Developmental trajectories and core regulatory networks were reconstructed, and essential transcription factors were functionally evaluated by computational vector field perturbations. The prognostic value of specific cellular states was assessed, and potential therapeutic antagonists were screened using computational databases and spatial molecular docking. Results Two distinct multidrug-resistant reservoirs were identified, an E2F1 -driven DNA repair state exhibiting cross-resistance to genotoxic agents, and a ZIC5 -regulated neuronal differentiation state associated with Hedgehog signaling. Trajectory inference and in silico perturbations demonstrated that the continuous accumulation of E2F1 is critical for maintaining the chemoresistant DNA repair phenotype. Clinical deconvolution revealed that elevated E2F1 expression acts as a robust indicator of poor overall survival. Subsequently, computational pharmacogenomic screening and molecular docking identified palbociclib as a highly potent inhibitor capable of precisely binding and targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis. Conclusion An E2F1 -driven DNA repair program and a ZIC5 -associated differentiation state directly govern distinct multidrug resistance mechanisms in MB. Targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis with palbociclib represents a promising precision therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in high-risk patients.

items.title: Kidzoi Enables Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory Activity and Variant Effect Prediction in Kidney
items.abstract_or_text: Sequence-to-function (S2F) deep learning models predict genome-wide functional profiles directly from DNA sequences and have significantly advanced our understanding of gene regulation. However, existing S2F models are fundamentally constrained by their initial training datasets, and no single model encompasses the full spectrum of cell types, clinical conditions, and cellular states, while training new models de novo is nontrivial. Here, we develop Kidzoi, a kidney cell-type-specific S2F model obtained by transfer learning from the pretrained model Borzoi using single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney tissue. Kidzoi accurately predicts cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and improves regulatory variant effect prediction in proximal tubule cells by up to 23% in terms of AUROC over existing models. Furthermore, Kidzoi effectively prioritizes genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapped causal variants associated with kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate based on both creatinine and cystatin C; eGFRcr-cys) while resolving their cell-type specificity. Systematic ablation of flanking sequence indicates that a local context of 32-64kbp, representing only 6-12% of the full model input, captures most of the information needed for variant effect prediction. Finally, we show that a multi-task model achieves comparable performance to single-task models at a substantially reduced computational cost.

items.title: APH-1A and CDK5 Expression Correlates with Tau Hyperphosphorylation and Its Attenuation by Brahmi and Donep-M in STZ induced Alzheimer’s Disease Model
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressively characterized neurodegenerative condition marked by molecular instability, neuronal dysfunction and abnormal tau buildup. Identification of disease-associated molecular signatures that can be experimentally validated in neuronal models may provide biologically relevant biomarkers and targets for therapeutic intervention. Here, we employed an integrated transcriptomic and cellular approach to identify and validate biomarkers associated with AD pathology. Differential transcriptomic analysis of (AD versus control) samples was used to prioritize candidate genes, followed by experimental validation in a streptozotocin (STZ) induced SH-SY5Y cells. Among the selected genes, anterior pharynx defective 1A (APH-1A) and cyclin dependent kinase (CDK5) were experimentally validated and further correlated to tau pathology by quantifying phosphorylation of tau at serine 396 (p-Tau Ser396) using confocal fluorescence microscopy. Complementary atomic force microscopy (AFM) was employed to characterize STZ-associated cellular morphological alterations. STZ exposure induced an AD-like neuronal phenotype characterized by associated cellular structural abnormalities. Importantly, co-treatment with (Brahmi) attenuated STZ-associated tau Ser396 phosphorylation and improved the cellular phenotype. The effects of Brahmi were further compared with those of established anti-Alzheimer’s drugs, Donep-M (Donepezil and Memantine) together, which similarly reduced p-Tau Ser396-associated alterations. The concordance between molecular biomarker validation and imaging-based phenotypic responses warrants further investigation of underlying molecular mechanisms. Collectively, our findings establish a transcriptome-to-cellular validation framework in which APH-1A and CDK5 represent experimentally supported AD-associated biomarkers. This integrated strategy provides a foundation for connecting human AD molecular signatures with measurable neuronal phenotypes and evaluating potential therapeutic interventions.

items.title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
items.abstract_or_text: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

items.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

items.title: Development and Internal Validation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults Undergoing Orthopaedic Surgery: A Prospective Cohort Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Objective Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common and serious complication following hip or knee replacement and revision surgery in older patients, leading to prolonged recovery, increased healthcare costs, and poor long-term outcomes. Early identification of high-risk patients remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and internally validate an interpretable machine learning (ML)-based risk prediction model for POD using multidimensional perioperative variables and to compare the predictive performance of seven ML algorithms. Methods This single-center prospective observational cohort study included 930 older patients (≥ 60 years) who underwent elective hip or knee replacement and revision surgery. POD was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) within 7 days after surgery. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection. Seven ML algorithms were developed and compared, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied for model interpretability. Results POD occurred in 30.0% (279/930) of patients. LASSO identified six predictors: preoperative sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, PSQI), psychological distress (Kessler Psychological Distress Scale, K10), social support (Groningen Orthopaedic Social Support Scale, GO-SSS), nutritional status (Prognostic Nutritional Index, PNI), comorbidity burden (age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index, aCCI), and intraoperative physiological reserve (Surgical Apgar Score, SAS). The extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) model performed best, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.922 (95% CI : 0.886–0.957) and a Brier score of 0.095. SHAP analysis revealed that preoperative sleep quality was the most influential predictor, showing a nonlinear positive association with POD risk and a synergistic interaction with psychological distress. Conclusion The XGBoost-based model integrating six readily available predictors demonstrated good predictive performance and potential clinical utility. The SHAP-based interpretability enhances model transparency, supporting early risk identification and personalized perioperative management. External validation is warranted to confirm generalizability.

items.title: Serum Hepatocyte Growth Factor Predicts Outcomes in Non-Acetaminophen Drug-Induced Acute Liver Failure.
items.abstract_or_text: Background and aims Regenerative capacity and inflammatory responses are key determinants of outcome in acute liver failure (ALF). However, their prognostic significance in non-acetaminophen drug-induced liver injury with acute liver injury or ALF (non-APAP-DILI-ALI/ALF) remains poorly defined. We aimed to identify biomarkers of regeneration and inflammation associated with clinical outcomes in this population. Methods We evaluated clinical laboratory parameters and circulating biomarkers in 79 patients with non-APAP-DILI-ALI/ALF (20 with ALI, 59 with ALF) and 19 healthy donors. We used multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of 21-day transplant-free survival among these patients. These predictors were used to create a composite model that was compared with the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score. Results Markers reflecting hepatic synthetic dysfunction (TBIL, INR, MELD) were strongly associated with the outcomes, whereas aminotransferases were not. HGF levels were markedly elevated in non-APAP-DILI-ALI/ALF patients versus healthy donors (5070 ± 4001 vs. 276 ± 581 pg/mL; p Conclusions HGF provides independent prognostic value beyond standard measures in non-APAP-DILI-ALF. The H-Score may improve risk stratification over the MELD score and warrants validation in a prospective cohort.

items.title: DreamFold: A World Model to efficiently generate protein folding pathways in the latent space.
items.abstract_or_text: While there is an abundance of static data for the structure of biological macromolecules, the data regarding their folding mechanisms and dynamics is scarce, posing a challenge to the training of AI models. The World Model approach, which has been very successful in robotics, can come in handy in this regard. From limited data, it can build a latent, approximated representation of the spatio-temporal folding environment that can be used to train downstream AI models. Here, we developed DreamFold, a World Model-based generative framework to perform biomolecular simulations. DreamFold encodes protein structures and dihedral angle moves into latent vectors using variational autoencoders. Then, it uses another neural network to rapidly predict the next latent structure after a latent move, allowing the model to develop its own understanding of protein dynamics. Finally, in a "hallucinated" latent environment, an agent learns, through evolutionary algorithms, a policy to drive folding simulations toward a target. Latent configurations can then be decoded back into atomistic structures. DreamFold can compute protein folding pathways four orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD), up to ~30,000×. Furthermore, for the monomeric proteins tested here (up to 449 aa), the computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms (N) as O(N) (in comparison, MD scales as O(NlogN)). We have validated our results against established MD benchmarks and other available experimental data. Finally, we show how DreamFold allows us to identify folding intermediates with cryptic binding sites that are therapeutically valuable. Overall, DreamFold facilitates the study of protein dynamics by generative AI with applications in structure-based drug discovery.

items.title: QuantCell: machine learning based cell annotation integrating qualitative and quantitative imaging profiles
items.abstract_or_text: Recent advances in spatial omics enable high-resolution, multiplexed imaging of RNA and protein expression, but cell annotation remains challenging, particularly in complex tissues with numerous markers or rare cell types. Here, we present QuantCell, a machine learning framework that leverages quantitative imaging data to improve annotation derived from qualitative profiles. QuantCell evaluates multiple models and applies a user-defined false discovery rate to ensure high-confidence annotation. Using PhenoCycler imaging of mouse bone marrow, QuantCell increased annotated cells from 33.1% to 90.2% at 5% FDR, achieving 96.5% accuracy. QuantCell supports diverse imaging platforms and robustly detects rare cell populations.

items.title: A decision-only model as a low-cost judge of medical AI answers
items.abstract_or_text: Background. Testing and deploying medical AI systems at scale already results in more outputs than clinicians can review, and the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges is growing rapidly. Decision-only models, cheap and fast models that return structured probabilities rather than text, offer a potentially scalable option for that goal. Methods. In an OSF pre-registered evaluation, we tested TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as a judge on tasks from five validated clinical benchmarks: rubric grading (HealthBench), planted clinical errors (When Rubrics Fail), risk in AI-written clinical documents (MedVAL), counseling ratings and failures (CounselBench) and physicians' preferences between answers (Real-POCQi). Comparators were expert raters' agreement with each other, OpenAI Decisions, GPT-6 Luna, a proposed hybrid team combining decision models and a cheap LLM and, as frontier comparators, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label. Results. The test comprised 25,091 units and 213,913 model calls. Jev's agreement with expert labels averaged 64.7% over six tasks. On 3,614 matched units it averaged 66.1%, against 65.0% for Opus and 60.7% for Sol, and it was non-inferior to both on four of six tasks. Jev judged the whole pool in 17 minutes for US1.46; per judgment, it cost 1/34 of Sol's price and 1/152 of Opus's. A preset cutoff held its false-alarm rate on fresh planted-error answers, and in simulation, reviewing Jev's least-sure answers first found 1.4 times the errors of a random audit. Still, omissions were hard for both: at the same false-alarm rate, Jev missed 55.6% of planted omissions and Opus 48.1%, and Opus caught 8.8 points more planted errors overall. Conclusions. Across more than 200,000 model calls, a decision-only model was non-inferior to two frontier judges on most tasks at a small fraction of their cost and time, while reporting how sure it was of every call. With local cutoffs and expert oversight of omissions and clinical documents, judging every output of a deployed medical AI system becomes more affordable.

items.title: Deep learning grading of Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis from ultrasound images: a weighted soft-voting ensemble of convolutional and transformer networks
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Schistosomiasis morbidity still persists in China despite extensive progress towards elimination of new and active infections. Diagnosis of liver fibrosis related to Schistosoma japonicum remains challenging due to the subjective nature of ultrasound grading and the shortage of experienced sonographers in endemic counties. Methods: We developed a deep learning model that grades schistosomal liver fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual delineation of a region of interest. We used 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18-88 years, median age 54 years; 46.4% female) from a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023. Of these, 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% had grade 0, 1, 2 and 3 fibrosis, respectively. Fibrosis grades were based on the clinical ultrasound record and re-evaluation by an experienced radiologist according to the Chinese Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control; discordant cases were reviewed by a second radiologist and resolved by consensus. Predictions from four neural networks with different architectures (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) were combined by weighted soft voting, with weights derived from validation performance. Results: For the four-grade task this model achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184-0.8856), an accuracy of 0.8500 (0.8136-0.8818) and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (0.8983-0.9373) on a fixed test set of 440 images. For detecting significant fibrosis (grade 2 or 3; test-set prevalence 0.530), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity was 0.9179, positive predictive value was 0.9300, negative predictive value was 0.9645, and AUROC was 0.9817. The ensemble achieved a higher macro-F1 than each individual backbone. Every ensemble misclassification was to an adjacent grade; no image with severe fibrosis was classified as no or mild fibrosis, or vice versa, whereas each individual backbone made 1-4 errors spanning two or more grades. Conclusions: The model may provide an automated aid for Schistosoma japonicum-associated fibrosis grading and could potentially support screening and follow-up in endemic areas after external validation.

items.title: Mitochondrial genome editing reveals the impact of complex I heteroplasmic variants on human neurogenesis
items.abstract_or_text: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants, whether maternally inherited or acquired somatically during aging, can be particularly detrimental to cells that rely on mitochondrial metabolism such as neurons. The functional consequences of mtDNA variants are thought to depend on their heteroplasmy, defined as the proportion of mtDNA molecules carrying that variant. However, investigating the specific effects of heteroplasmic mtDNA variants on human neuronal function has been challenging. Studies using patient-derived cells cannot conclusively attribute observed phenotypes to a single mtDNA variant, while conventional genome editing approaches are not applicable to mtDNA. Here, we use DddA-derived cytosine base editor (DdCBE) to introduce pathogenic heteroplasmic mtDNA variants into Neurogenin 2 (NGN2)-inducible human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We focus on two variants in the genes MT-ND1 and MT-ND5 belonging to complex I (CI), the largest component of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and a frequent contributor to human disease, including the incurable neurodevelopmental disorder Leigh syndrome. mtDNA-edited iPSC lines exhibit low off-target editing and maintain similar heteroplasmy following subclonal isolation and differentiation into NGN2-induced neurons (iNs). Although the CI variants do not substantially affect mitochondrial energy metabolism in undifferentiated iPSCs, they reduce mitochondrial membrane potential in iNs where they drive a transcriptional reprogramming indicative of impaired neuronal commitment. These findings suggest that heteroplasmic CI variants are sufficient to disrupt neural fate specification even at relatively low heteroplasmy. More broadly, mtDNA editing in human iPSCs provides a powerful platform to investigate how mitochondrial fitness and heteroplasmy influence development and disease.

items.title: Convergent genome- and gene-level constraints shape repeated environmental adaptation in grasses
items.abstract_or_text: Grasses (Poaceae) dominate terrestrial ecosystems and sustain global food security, yet the genomic principles enabling their repeated adaptation to extreme environments remain unresolved. Combining dense phylogenomic sampling, global environmental data, and genomic large language models (gLLMs), we characterize the mutational targets underlying environmental shift across 687 genomes from 561 species spanning 17 climate zones. We identify 17-30 phylogenetically independent transitions into extreme temperature, water, and soil environments, accompanied by convergent shifts in genome-scale molecular properties, including the Nitrogen-to-Carbon balance and the biosynthetic cost of the proteome. Our gLLMs-informed phylogenetic mixed modeling framework identifies 330 genes that repeatedly associated with distinct axes of environmental variation, highlighting the importance of protein modification and localization within extracellular and organellar compartments. Overlaying independent convergent selection tests identifies 27 high-confidence candidates for further characterization. Together, our results show that grass adaptation is canalized by layered constraints at genome-wide and gene-specific scales, producing predictable evolutionary trajectories.

items.title: The Findings Workflow: An agentic, collaborative, provenance-tracked framework for scientific data analysis with Claude Code
items.abstract_or_text: Scientists presented with quantitative data often face two related problems: confidence that an analysis is statistically and computationally correct, and provenance sufficient to reproduce the resulting figures and conclusions. Large language models (LLMs) can make sophisticated analyses accessible through a collaborative, conversational interface, but unstructured use can worsen both problems by producing plausible but incorrect results and obscuring the steps that produced them. Here we present the Findings Workflow, a free, open-source Claude Code plugin designed to retain the flexibility of conversational LLM-assisted analysis while placing it within a structured, verifiable, and reproducible environment. The workflow uses staged, gated progression to ensure the science, metadata, and data are understood and tested data loaders are built before downstream analysis begins. Specialized subagents perform statistical analysis, programming, visualization, research, reporting, and validation, with independent review incorporated throughout. The plugin also provides vetted analysis templates, conventions, and methodological guidance that serve as trusted sources of opinion when deciding how analyses should be performed. Scientists remain actively involved throughout, exploring their data and directing the analysis through natural-language conversation, while the workflow supplies structure, verification, and persistent state around that collaboration. Findings are recorded automatically together with the data, code, methods, figures, and provenance needed to reproduce them. We demonstrate the workflow with a worked example that reproduces central findings from a published plasma extracellular vesicle proteomics dataset examining Alzheimer's disease (Mag-Net). Together, these features are designed to make LLM-assisted scientific analysis easier to trust, inspect, and reproduce without sacrificing its conversational and exploratory nature.

items.title: Batch Effect Correction to Enhance Utility of a Publicly Available ALS Proteomics Dataset
items.abstract_or_text: Large, publicly available databases of patient data have been successful in identifying associations between neurodegenerative diseases and biological features that might otherwise go unnoticed. The Answer ALS Consortium is one such database that has generated a rich repository of multi-omic data from people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, large studies can suffer from batch effects that obscure genuine biological signal and prevent experiment reproducibility. In this study, we identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS 1-2 proteomic dataset (508 samples x 3,643 proteins) and corrected the effect using both the internal controls provided by Answer ALS and the batch effect-correction algorithm (BECA) ComBat. We identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS Dataset 1-2 proteomic dataset that, uncorrected, may obscure biology. Proteins MOS and H4 were outliers of expression in the dataset that correlated with the batch effect. Removing MOS and H4 did not correct the effect fully but did reveal new principal component (PC) contributing proteins related to motor neurons and potentially ALS: AINX, NFL, and NFM. The batch differential controls (BDCs) provided by Answer ALS were used to correct samples in their respective batches. ComBat, a well-characterized BECA, was applied to the dataset both before (ComBat-BDC) and after (BDC-ComBat) correction with the BDCs. BDC-ComBat was the only method that successfully reduced batch effect across the entire dataset. This method also preserved four of the top six PC-contributing proteins from the original dataset, including three neuronal proteins, suggesting that the corrected dataset recapitulates biology as well as the variability of the original dataset. Altogether, we produced a version of the Answer ALS proteomic dataset (354 samples by 3,641 proteins) with globally reduced batch effect and protein-level reduced batch effect. This version of the dataset recapitulates the individual protein variability and important neuronal proteins of the original. We also created a workflow for identifying and correcting batch effects that can be applied to other large data repositories.

items.title: Applications of large language model in general practice: a qualitative interview study with professionals and patients
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Workload is increasing in general practice. Large language models (LLMs) are a promising tool that could relieve part of this workload. However, existing studies offer little insight into how professionals and patients want specific LLM applications to be implemented in practice. Objectives: This study aimed to prioritize a broad range of LLM applications in general practice and identify the benefits, risks, and requirements of each application. Methods: We conducted semi-structured one-on-one interviews with 12 general practitioners (GPs), 7 GP assistants, 6 practice nurses, and 6 patient representatives in the Netherlands between October and December 2025. To guide the interviews, we developed a list of 21 LLM applications derived from literature, existing tools, and GP input. Application were divided into 5 categories: administrative tasks, pre-consultation and triage, clinical decision support, management of (chronic) diseases, and patient interaction and communication. Participants discussed and prioritized each application. Transcripts were analyzed with a combined deductive and inductive approach. Results: Priorities for LLM applications differed by group: GPs favored clinical decision support, assistants favored triage, and practice nurses and patient representatives favored chronic disease management. The most prioritized applications were summarizing consultations and triage and urgency classification (high priority 18/31; 58%), followed by clarification of medical information around the consultation (14/31; 45%). The qualitative analysis revealed three recurring considerations when applying LLMs for different tasks. First, participants questioned whether an LLM is needed, as simpler or existing tools may suffice. Second, they questioned whether LLMs relieve workload or create extra work. Third, a possible benefit on workload has to explicitly be weighed against risks such as mistakes, reduced personal care and accessibility, and negative effects on professionals. Conclusions: Professionals and patients see potential for LLM support across many areas of general practice. Realizing this potential requires three steps: critically assessing whether an LLM is the right tool, establishing that it relieves workload, and designing applications so that their benefits outweigh the risks. Our application-level prioritization and analysis provide a starting point for assessment and design.

items.title: Inflammatory biomarker candidates in dementia with Lewy bodies: diagnostic classification, clinical associations, and survival
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is a common neurodegenerative dementia that remains difficult to distinguish clinically from Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related disorders because of overlapping clinical features and frequent mixed pathology. Because alpha-synuclein pathology is associated with central and peripheral immune alterations, targeted measurement of inflammation-related biomarker candidates may provide a minimally invasive means of characterizing disease biology and supporting differential diagnosis. We examined whether plasma concentrations of proteins on the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel differed between participants with DLB (n = 20), mild cognitive impairment and/or AD (MCI+/AD; n = 15), and cognitively normal controls (n = 15), and assessed their associations with clinical measures and survival. Differential-expression analyses, covariate-adjusted logistic regression with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, protein-clinical correlations, survival analyses, and pathway enrichment analyses were performed. No protein survived false-discovery-rate correction; nominal associations therefore describe exploratory signals. Relative to controls, DLB showed nominally higher CCL20 and CXCL11. Compared with MCI+/AD, DLB showed nominally lower MCP-2 and IL-2 and higher IL-18R1, TRANCE, GDNF, and IL-12B. AUCs derived from multivariable logistic models containing each protein and prespecified covariates ranged from 0.853 to 0.890 for the DLB versus MCI+/AD comparison. Higher TRANCE was nominally associated with greater motor severity (UPDRS: rho = 0.41, p = 0.0176), whereas its associations with ACE-R and MMSE did not reach nominal significance. Survival analyses identified limited and imprecise associations over a median follow-up of 6.5 years (range 0.07–9.80; IQR 3.49–7.93 years). Pathway analyses highlighted immune and intracellular signaling networks, including NF-kB and MAPK signaling. These exploratory findings support a targeted peripheral inflammatory signature in DLB that differs from normal ageing and MCI+/AD but require validation in larger independent cohorts.

items.title: Drug-Specific Associations of Angiotensin Receptor Blockers With Parkinson's Disease Risk in a Multicenter Electronic Health Record Cohort.
items.abstract_or_text: Background Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) have demonstrated neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of Parkinson's disease (PD), but individual ARBs differ in pharmacological properties that may influence their neuroprotective potential. Objectives Using large-scale hospital electronic health records of the University of California health system, we tested whether specific ARBs are associated with lower PD risk. Methods We conducted a new-user, active-comparator cohort study in the University of California Health Data Warehouse, encompassing 890 712 hypertensive patients across six academic medical centers from 2012 to 2025. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios for individual ARB associations with incident PD, adjusting for demographics, nine preindex comorbidities, and index date. Robustness was assessed through propensity score matching and negative-control analysis. Results Drug-specific Cox analysis identified irbesartan (HR = 0.588, 95% CI 0.434 to 0.796, p = 0.0006) and olmesartan (HR = 0.797, 95% CI 0.665 to 0.956, p = 0.015) as associated with lower PD risk. Irbesartan survived Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and propensity score matching supported both associations. Conclusion In this large multicenter EHR cohort, irbesartan and olmesartan were associated with lower incident Parkinson's disease risk. These findings support further investigation of the renin-angiotensin system as a therapeutic target in Parkinson's disease and may inform the development or repurposing of agents with favorable central nervous system penetration and neuroprotective potential.

items.title: Machine Learning Estimation of Gestational Age at Delivery Using Linked Mother-Infant Electronic Health Records Across Two Health Systems.
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose This study aimed to develop and evaluate machine-learning models for estimating gestational age at delivery using EHR data from two health systems. Methods We trained random forest, gradient boosting, and ensemble models using EHR data from mother-infant dyads at Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) and independently reimplemented and retrained the modeling pipeline at the University of Michigan (UMich). We further analyzed EHR predictors of gestational age, assessed temporal drift in EHR data elements, and evaluated model performance stratified by gestational-age category at delivery. Results The study included pregnancies corresponding to 54 344 and 34 345 mother-infant dyads at VUMC (2005-2025) and UMich (2012-2024), respectively. The gestational age predictions of the ensemble models showed high agreement with the reference standard on the VUMC dataset (±1 week: 85.1%, ±2 weeks: 94.3%, MAE: 4.4 days). When the same modeling pipeline was independently implemented and retrained on the UMich dataset, the ensemble models achieved higher agreement with the reference standard (±1 week: 93.1%, ±2 weeks: 97.8%, MAE: 2.8 days). Further, performance was better among pregnancies delivered in more recent years, and among full- and late-term deliveries compared with preterm deliveries. Discussion The results indicate that supervised machine learning methods leveraging linked mother-infant EHRs can accurately estimate gestational age at delivery overall, although performance was substantially lower for preterm deliveries. Reproducibility of the modeling approach and portability of the analytic workflow were demonstrated across the two health systems. Conclusion This study presents a robust machine learning framework to estimate gestational age at delivery, whose development process was reproducible across two health systems. The framework has the potential to support large-scale real-world maternal and neonatal health studies requiring retrospective estimation of gestational age.

items.title: Automated Multienzyme Digestion Workflows for Confident Characterization of Challenging Posttranslational Modifications in Therapeutic Antibodies by LC-MS/MS.
items.abstract_or_text: Rationale Non-reduced trypsin digestion of therapeutic antibodies can generate large disulfide-linked peptide complexes that exhibit poor chromatographic and mass spectrometric performance. This limits the confident characterization of posttranslational modifications (PTMs) in specific antibody regions, such as the heavy-chain constant region 1 (CH1) domain, where conventional digestion produces 8-kDa complexes with poor fragmentation. Methods We developed automated multistep and multienzyme digestion workflows using immobilized trypsin, chymotrypsin, and proteinase K on magnetic beads. These workflows were implemented on a robotic platform and evaluated for their ability to characterize engineered cysteine residues in the CH1 domain of antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) intermediates. Analysis was performed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Results The multienzyme workflows generated highly orthogonal peptide pools; for instance, selected workflows using trypsin only, trypsin combined with chymotrypsin, and trypsin combined with proteinase K yielded 13%, 14%, and 34% unique peptide identifications, respectively. In the challenging CH1 region, the multienzyme approach identified six distinct cysteine adducts at engineered Cys152. These included cysteinylation, homocysteinylation, and an unexpected, putative process-related impurity, thioglycolic acid capping, which was validated with unambiguous MS and MS/MS evidence using selected multienzyme workflows. Relative extracted-ion current-based levels of these cappings were observed and found to be similar across selected workflows; for instance, relative levels of thioglycolic acid capping from 12% to 15% were observed across selected workflows. Conclusions The presented automated multienzyme workflows serve as complementary tools in an analytical toolbox, which can be strategically deployed for targeting challenging regions of biopharmaceutical products. We demonstrate significantly improved precursor signal quality and MS/MS sequence coverage compared to trypsin-only protocols. The presented workflows are fast (36-92 min total runtime) and utilize commercially available reagents and instrumentation, making them suitable for direct implementation in biopharmaceutical analytical development and quality control laboratories.

items.title: Explainable temporal machine learning of multimorbidity trajectories after acute myocardial infarction: complementing clinical risk scores with mechanistic phenotypes.
items.abstract_or_text: Objective This study aimed to identify trajectories of multimorbidity following acute myocardial infarction (AMI), using explainable temporal machine-learning methods, and assess their clinical, prognostic, and biological significance. Materials and methods Dynamic Time Warping k-means clustering was applied to post-AMI diagnostic sequences from 12 701 UK-Biobank participants. Latent Dirichlet Allocation characterised cluster themes. Multiclass classifiers (CatBoost, XGBoost, random forest, logistic regression) trained on pre-AMI diagnoses and demographics predicted trajectory membership, with SHAP interpretability. SMART scores and Cox models evaluated 5-year mortality; Phenotype-Wide Association (PheWAS) and Reactome pathway enrichment were used to identify associated biological mechanisms. Results Three trajectories of multimorbidity were identified: acute cardiorenal-respiratory with metabolic disease (ACUTE-CARD; 63.4%), cardiometabolic disease with arrhythmic-ischemic burden (CARDIOMIX; 13.5%), and smoking-related multisystem multimorbidity (SMO-CARD; 23.1%). XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUC-ROC 0.906; 95% CI, 0.895-0.916), with CatBoost showing comparable performance (AUC-ROC 0.900; 95% CI, 0.889-0.910). SMO-CARD had the highest 5-year mortality (43.9%). The established SMART cardiovascular risk score remained the dominant predictor of mortality while the identified trajectories provided complementary prognostic signals; these associations were weaker after full adjustment for potential confounders with each profile displaying distinct genetic and pathway signatures. Discussion The SMART score outperformed in capturing mortality risk, whereas the trajectories complement it by revealing nuanced clustering of risk factors across organ systems and in identifying trajectory-specific intervention priorities. Conclusion Explainable temporal modeling of EHR data reveals clinically interpretable, biologically grounded multimorbidity trajectories after AMI that complement established risk scores and provide a reproducible approach to mechanistic phenotyping and precision care.

items.title: Biologically grounded locality priors close the data gap for vision transformers in neural prediction
items.abstract_or_text: For datasets with thousands of neurons and images, vision transformers have proven successful at predicting neural responses to stimuli. However, they are expected to underperform in low-data regimes, where CNNs and Gaussian processes are considered more effective. We ask whether transformers can be made competitive for small-scale neural prediction, and show that underperformance in this regime can be overturned with the right inductive bias. We equip a vision transformer with a differentiable per-neuron circular crop in feature space. The crop is centered on each neuron's receptive field, with a radius selected per neuron, so the model only sees the small image region that drives that neuron instead of the whole image. This makes the cost of attention scale with the size of the receptive field rather than with the size of the image. A single transformer stack is shared across all neurons: each neuron's specificity resides in the crop, not in the architecture. We call this model circular receptive-field vision transformer (CiRF-ViT). We evaluate it on small multi-electrode-array recordings of mouse and salamander retinas: a mouse preparation of 41 ganglion cells and two salamander preparations totaling 49 ganglion cells, each with only a few thousand stimulus-response pairs, two orders of magnitude below the scale at which transformers are typically trained. Against CNN and Gaussian-process baselines, CiRF-ViT reaches the highest mean explained variance on both datasets (0.94 on mouse, 0.95 on salamander). Probed with the local spike-triggered average (LSTA), a zero-shot test of context-dependent, nonlinear stimulus sensitivity, CiRF-ViT reproduces the qualitative polarity inversion that a linear model cannot capture by construction. A biologically grounded, per-neuron locality prior is therefore enough to make transformers competitive for neural prediction well below their usual data scale, while matching the reference models on an established functional signature of the retina's nonlinear computation.

items.title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility
items.abstract_or_text: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

items.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
items.abstract_or_text: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers.
